t: Find Number of Coins to Place in Tree Nodes
o: For each node, consider all triples of distinct nodes in its subtree and place the maximum product (or 0 if every product is negative); subtrees of size < 3 get 1 coin. The maximum product of three values is either the product of the three largest values, or (two most-negative values) × (largest value). So each subtree only needs its top-3 maxima and top-2 minima — mergeable bottom-up in O(1)-ish per child.
k: Max product of 3 numbers = max(top3 product, min1*min2*max1).
Keep only 3 largest and 2 smallest values per subtree; merging child summaries suffices.
Process nodes in reverse BFS order so all children are finalized before their parent.

a.n: Bottom-up tree DP with top-3/top-2 summaries
a.i: Root the tree at 0, get a BFS order, and process it reversed. Each node merges its own cost with its children's (max3, min2) lists, truncates to 3 and 2 respectively, tracks subtree size, and computes coins. Leaves naturally get size 1 → 1 coin.
s: Build adjacency, BFS from root 0 recording parents and an order.
Reverse-iterate the order: gather candidate values from self and children.
Sort candidates, keep top-3 and bottom-2, accumulate subtree size.
If size < 3 answer 1; else answer max(top3 product, twoMins * max) clamped at 0.
a.t: O(n log n) — each node sorts O(deg·5) candidates; total work is linear times a small constant log factor.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency, order, and per-node summary lists.

w: Products reach 1e4³ = 1e12, so use 64-bit integers (BigInt in JS for safety). Recursion risks stack overflow on a 2e4-deep chain — the iterative BFS-order trick avoids it. Pitfall: forgetting the negative case yields 0 coins, not the negative product, and that size < 3 always means exactly 1 coin even with huge costs. Follow-up: k largest instead of 3, or rerooting queries.
